messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Welder
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 52

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Auditory (Cars): Car sounds
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Memory → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Tevita, a 51‑year‑old welder from the island of Viti Levu, spent most of his life in the glow of molten metal, the hiss of welding torches, and the steady rhythm of steel being joined. He and his wife, Aroha, had lived in a modest house for fifteen years, the sound of cars and trucks the soundtrack of their daily routine. One rainy evening in August, while driving home from a late shift, Tevita’s life turned on its head. A drunk driver, the seat of his car slipping into a lane that was closed for construction, slammed into the rear of Tevita’s vehicle. The impact was sudden and violent, the steering wheel buckling, metal cracking. He was thrown forward, his body pressed against the seat, his head striking the dashboard. The world exploded into noise: metal screeching, glass shattering, and a sudden, acrid smell of burning plastic. He emerged from the wreck, wounded, but alive. After the crash, the memory of that night did not fade. Instead, it settled into the deeper parts of his mind, a place where the scene could be replayed with alarming clarity. Whenever the sight of a car in a traffic jam, a news clip of a collision, or even a faint hum of an engine on the radio surfaced, Tevita’s body would snap back into the position he had held that night, his back and shoulders tense, his heart racing. The physical pain that had been lodged in his ribs during the crash returned in pulses, sharp and familiar, as if the injury had never healed. In those moments the memory was not simply a recollection; it was a full sensory reliving, complete with the smell of gasoline, the screeching of tires, and the metallic taste of blood on his tongue. When the memory surfaces, the triggers that had become inextricably linked to the event flare up automatically. The vividness of the scene pulls in the crash imagery: the sight of cars hitting each other, the flash of flashing lights, the blackened wreckage. The odor of alcohol, which Tevita had been exposed to at the bar that night before the crash, clings to the air, stirring a sense of danger and dread. The roar of engines and the clatter of clutches in traffic echo in his mind, making the world around him feel like an arena of imminent catastrophe. In one paragraph that a therapist could have written, it is clear that the memory of the collision gives rise to the triggers: “When the memory of the collision surfaces, the vivid body position and pain immediately ignite the crash imagery and car sounds that had become triggers, bringing the present environment into that terrifying moment.” The welding shop, once a sanctuary of focused labor, has become a minefield of stimuli that threaten to reopen the trauma. The hiss of the welding arc, the clanging of metal, and even the faint metallic tang of solder all echo the sounds Tevita had once heard on the highway. Whenever the shop’s lights flicker and the sound of an engine starts outside the workshop, he feels a jolt that forces him to retreat from the workbench. He has begun arriving late or skipping early shifts, telling his supervisor that he needs to check the truck’s oil or that the engine sounds are too loud. Aroha notices the change; she sees him pull back into the living room after the workday, avoiding the garage entirely. Tevita, for the first time since the crash, avoids the very environment that once defined his identity. Weeks turned into months, and the pattern of feeling the body in that same position, the pain returning, and the sensory flood that flooded the present grew more entrenched. The welding shop’s sounds became less tolerable, the traffic outside his window a constant reminder of the collision’s echoes. He began to dread the simple act of driving, the routine that had once been a safe commute. The weight of the unresolved memories and the intensity of the triggers had begun to sap his energy, leaving him exhausted even after a full day at work. It is this mounting anxiety and the fear of losing his livelihood that finally led Tevita to seek help. He worries that if he cannot return to the shop, he will lose his sense of purpose and his connection to his wife and family. He hopes to find a way to stay grounded in the present, to keep the memory from commandeering his life, and to reclaim the sound of his own heartbeat without the echo of a crash. He brings his story to the therapist with a trembling voice, asking, “I don’t want to live like this—stuck in a loop of pain and danger. I just want to put my hand on the welding torch again without my heart pounding like it’s the end of the world.”
